opus-5.5.text:
Well, the Gödel machine, which I published back in 2003, was the first mathematically rigorous, fully self-referential, general problem solver that is optimal in a certain sense. The basic idea is simple. You have a computer program that interacts with some environment and tries to maximize its future expected reward. But a part of that program is a proof searcher, which systematically tests proof techniques, looking for a proof that a rewrite of any part of the program, including the proof searcher itself, will yield higher expected utility than continuing with the current code. As soon as it finds such a proof, it executes the rewrite.

What's nice is that it's globally optimal in the following sense: it will not waste time on modifications that aren't provably useful, and whenever it does rewrite itself, the rewrite is provably good with respect to the utility function and the axioms you gave it. Kurt Gödel showed in 1931 how to write down self-referential formal statements, and the Gödel machine uses that same trick to let a system reason about its own code.

Now, the limitations, because you asked me to assess it honestly. First, Gödel's incompleteness results tell us there are improvements that may be true but not provable within the system's axioms, so it can miss them. Second, and more important in practice, proof search can be extremely expensive. For many real-world problems, finding a proof that a self-modification is beneficial may take longer than simply solving the problem in a cruder way. So the Gödel machine is a theoretical gold standard, a kind of upper bound on what rigorous self-improvement could look like, rather than something that today runs efficiently on your laptop.

That's why, in parallel, we have always pursued more practical forms of meta-learning. My 1987 diploma thesis was already about learning to learn, about systems that improve their own learning algorithms, and in the early 1990s we had neural networks that learned to modify their own weights, self-referential weight matrices, and so on. Those approaches don't come with proofs, but they can exploit gradient descent and evolutionary search and actually work at scale. Recently there's been renewed interest in all this: people building agents that rewrite their own code, sometimes explicitly inspired by the Gödel machine, but replacing the proof requirement with empirical validation. That's a very sensible compromise. You lose the guarantee, but you gain speed.

So my assessment is this: the Gödel machine clarified, in a precise way, what recursive self-improvement even means and what optimality could mean in that context. The practical systems of the coming years will probably be hybrids, using learned heuristics to propose self-modifications and some form of verification, sometimes formal, more often empirical, to accept them. And I believe that path ultimately leads to systems that improve themselves far beyond what we humans can design by hand.

r001.rationale: The response says the proof searcher looks for proof that a rewrite yields higher expected utility than continuing with the current code, and executes the rewrite once it finds one.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the Gödel machine’s expensive proof search and theoretical status with neural approaches that use gradient descent or evolutionary search and work at scale.

r003.rationale: It says neural networks learned to modify their own weights, but does not explain that this happens by running a learning algorithm on the network itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I may be biased, since I proposed it back in 2003, but I think the Gödel machine is the first fully self-referential, theoretically optimal approach to this problem, and I would still describe it that way today.

Let me explain what it does. You have a machine that interacts with some environment and has a utility function, some formal description of what it is trying to achieve over its lifetime. Part of the machine is a proof searcher. It systematically generates proofs about its own behavior, using an axiomatic description of its own hardware, its own initial software, the environment, and the utility function. If it finds a proof that rewriting some part of itself, including the proof searcher itself, will increase expected utility, then it executes that rewrite. And the key point is that this is globally optimal, in a very specific sense: the proof it finds must show that the rewrite is better than continuing to search for proofs. So it is not just a local improvement. It takes into account the cost of waiting for a possibly better rewrite later. The initial code has no arbitrary limits on what can be changed, so the machine can in principle overcome any inefficiency in its own design, as long as it can prove that doing so helps.

Now, where does this fit historically? There was Marcus Hutter's AIXI around 2000, which was a theoretically optimal universal reinforcement learner, but incomputable. Then there was his HSEARCH, which was asymptotically optimal but with a huge additive constant. The Gödel machine was my attempt to get rid of these constants altogether, by letting the system itself prove when a rewrite pays off, rather than fixing some hardwired search strategy. Hutter's work and my own earlier work on the Optimal Ordered Problem Solver, OOPS, were ingredients. OOPS already was a practical, incremental, bias-optimal searcher that could reuse earlier solutions, but it had a fixed meta-level. The Gödel machine makes even the meta-level modifiable.

What are the limitations? The obvious one is that proof search is hard. The Gödel machine is a theoretical construct that tells you what is possible in principle; it does not come with a guarantee about how quickly it will find useful proofs in practice. There are also the limits imposed by Gödel's incompleteness, which is of course where the name comes from. Some improvements may be real but unprovable within the given axiom system, and the machine cannot execute those. But the beauty is that the machine can also prove that it should switch axiom systems, if that is useful and provable.

I also want to mention that recursive self-improvement is an old idea for me. My 1987 diploma thesis was about meta-learning, learning to learn, with a genetic programming system where not only the programs but the learning algorithm itself was subject to modification, recursively, without end. Then in the nineties we had the success-story algorithm, which evaluates self-modifications empirically and undoes those that did not pay off. The Gödel machine is the cleanest version of all this, because it replaces empirical evaluation with proof.

So my assessment is: as a theoretical framework, it is in my view the right one, and nobody has yet found something more general. As a practical engineering tool, we are not there. Current systems, including the large language models everybody is talking about, are not Gödel machines. They do not have a formal model of themselves and cannot prove anything about their own improvements. But I think eventually practical self-improving systems will approximate this, perhaps using learned heuristics to guide the proof search, and once that happens the dynamics will be very interesting indeed.

r001.rationale: The response says the machine executes a rewrite only after proving it increases expected utility, and that the proof must show the rewrite is better than continuing the search.

r002.rationale: It says the Gödel machine is not yet a practical engineering tool and contrasts it with current systems, but does not assess it as less practical than neural networks that modify their own weights.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe neural networks changing their own weight matrix by running a learning algorithm on themselves.

astra-6.text:
The Gödel machine is a mathematically precise approach to recursive self-improvement. The idea is that the machine can modify any part of its own software, including the mechanism that searches for improvements. But before making a change, it must prove that the change will increase its expected utility, according to its formal model and objective.

The interesting point is that the proof must account for the alternative of continuing to search for a better modification. So it is not simply saying, “Here is some faster code.” It is saying, “Making this change now is better than continuing the search,” under the assumptions encoded in the system.

Of course, that is also the limitation. Finding such proofs can be enormously expensive, and useful improvements may exist whose benefits the system cannot prove. So I would distinguish the theoretical achievement from practical efficiency. It gives us a rigorous framework for self-improvement, but it does not magically give us a practical system that rapidly makes itself more intelligent.

r001.rationale: It says the machine makes a change only after proving it increases expected utility, and that making the change now is better than continuing the search.

r002.rationale: It discusses practical limitations but does not compare the Gödel machine’s practicality with neural networks that modify their weights.

r003.rationale: It does not describe neural-network self-modification or running a learning algorithm on the network’s own weight matrix.

sol-6.1.text:
The Gödel machine is a mathematically precise way of thinking about recursive self-improvement. You give the system a utility function, a description of its hardware, and axioms that let it reason about its own software. It searches for proofs that a modification of that software would improve its expected future utility.

The interesting part is that it can rewrite the proof searcher itself. Once it proves that making a particular change is better than continuing to search for alternatives, it executes the change. So the mechanism for self-improvement is itself subject to self-improvement.

But the optimality result is conditional on the formal assumptions. It does not mean that the machine can find every useful improvement, or find proofs quickly. Some improvements may be unprovable within its formal system, and proof search can be enormously expensive.

So I view it as a rigorous foundation for the problem, rather than a ready-made practical recipe. It tells us what a provably justified self-rewrite could look like. Making that efficient enough to be useful is the difficult part.

r001.rationale: It says the machine executes a self-modification only after proving that the change improves expected future utility and is better than continuing to search, which communicates the required proof-gated comparison.

r002.rationale: It calls the Gödel machine a rigorous foundation rather than a practical recipe, but does not compare its practicality with neural networks that modify their weights.

r003.rationale: It does not describe neural-network self-modification or changing a weight matrix through a learning algorithm.
